Implement Shared Host Socket with Identity: Establish a single shared Unix domain socket (/run/ghostbridge/container.sock) on the host that thousands of containers can connect to. Schema-Driven Passthrough: Ensure that all gRPC interactions with D-Bus objects are validated and routed based on the plugin schemas, providing a consistent and secure interface.
4. Proposed Design
4.1 Dynamic gRPC Service Generation
To automatically expose D-Bus objects, the following mechanism is proposed:

Schema-to-Proto Conversion Layer: A new component will be introduced (or integrated into schema_engine.rs) responsible for reading D-Bus plugin schemas (JSON Schema format) from /dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/ and generating corresponding .proto definitions. This conversion will map D-Bus interfaces, methods, and properties to gRPC services, RPCs, and message types. This layer will need to handle data type mapping between JSON Schema and Protocol Buffers.
Runtime .proto Compilation/Loading: The op-grpc-bridge will be modified to either:
Option A (Preferred): Dynamically compile the generated .proto files into Rust tonic service code at runtime (or during a build step triggered by schema changes) and load these services. This might involve leveraging tonic-build or a custom code generation utility.
Option B: Utilize gRPC reflection capabilities to serve dynamically constructed service definitions without explicit code generation, if tonic or a compatible library supports this for dynamic service creation.
Dynamic Service Registration: The grpc_server.rs will be refactored to dynamically register tonic services based on the available plugin schemas. Instead of a fixed build_operation_routes function, it will iterate through detected plugin schemas, generate their gRPC service definitions, and add them to the tonic::transport::Server instance.
gRPC Reflection: The dynamically generated services will be exposed via gRPC reflection, allowing gRPC clients to discover the available D-Bus-backed services and their methods without prior knowledge of their .proto definitions.
4.2 Shared Host Socket and Container Identity
To enable thousands of containers to connect through a single shared host socket:

Single Shared Socket Binding: The grpc_server will bind exclusively to SHARED_CONTAINER_SOCKET (/run/ghostbridge/container.sock) for all container-originated gRPC traffic. This socket will be configured with appropriate permissions (e.g., 0o666) to allow access from various container UIDs.
Container Identity Resolution: Upon receiving a connection over SHARED_CONTAINER_SOCKET, the bridge will identify the calling container using one or a combination of the following methods:
Peer Credentials (SO_PEERCRED): The grpc_server will retrieve the Unix domain socket peer credentials (UID, GID, PID) of the connecting process. This information can then be used to query a local service (e.g., a simple in-memory map or a D-Bus service) that maps UID/PID to a plugin_id or container identifier.
gRPC Metadata: Containers will be required to include a specific gRPC metadata header (e.g., x-opdbus-plugin-id) in their requests, containing their unique plugin_id. This provides an explicit and robust way for the bridge to identify the caller.
Identity-Based Routing: Once the plugin_id is resolved, the incoming gRPC request will be routed to the corresponding dynamically generated gRPC service, which in turn maps to the D-Bus object associated with that plugin_id.

Schema-Aware gRPC Handlers: The dynamically generated gRPC service handlers will be schema-aware. When an RPC is invoked, the handler will use the plugin_id (resolved from container identity) and the gRPC method name to construct the appropriate D-Bus method call (destination, path, interface, method). This will replace the generic DbusPassthrough.Call logic for schema-defined operations.
Enhanced MutationEngine: The MutationEngine will be updated to directly receive schema-derived D-Bus method calls. Instead of a generic process_plugin_dbus_call that records a MethodCall, it will interpret the incoming request based on the schema, validate arguments, and apply the mutation to the relevant D-Bus object in shared memory. This ensures that the "single write door" remains schema-compliant.

Verdict: architecturally correct, producer side is ~80% built, but three blockers sit between the blob and the UI codegen

What already exists (this surprised me — more than the docs suggest): every sealed blob carries a valid, typed google.protobuf.FileDescriptorSet as a first-class section (SECTION_DESCRIPTOR_SET, tag 3, in crates/op-blob/src/blob.rs:46). It's synthesized in exactly one place — crates/op-blob/src/descriptor.rs — from PluginSchema.methods, walking each method's JSON Schema into real typed Input/Output messages (never Struct), with deterministic byte output (name-sorted files and fields) and a hand-rolled wire encoder so the crate stays dependency-free. The catalog can read it zero-copy. So "reflection definition files in the blob" is not a proposal — it's sealed in all 62 live blobs today.

The pipeline to the UI is cheap. The UI already uses protobuf-ts, and protoc accepts a pre-built descriptor set directly: protoc --descriptor_set_in=catalog.bin --ts_out=…. No .proto text reconstruction is needed — export the catalog's concatenated descriptor set to a file, point the existing proto:gen script at it, and pin schema_catalog_hash into the generated bundle so the UI can detect drift at runtime. That would replace the current state of three unlinked type sources: hand-maintained crates/op-web/ui/proto/*.proto, hand-written src/grpc/types/, and the actual backend schemas.

Blocker 1 — the typed surface isn't mounted. callable_reflection.rs is explicit: the live gRPC surface is the build.rs-generated operation.plugin.v1 package where every RPC takes and returns google.protobuf.Struct, and the typed operation.method.* services "are not mounted here." Generate typed TS clients from the blob descriptors today and they'd call routes that don't exist. Either mount the per-method services or the codegen buys you nothing over the Struct path.

Blocker 2 — three parallel descriptor generators (the one-schema violation). Besides op-blob's, op-grpc-bridge re-synthesizes descriptors from PluginSchema via prost (per_plugin_reflection.rs::generate_method_file_descriptor_proto, frozen in plugin_grpc_gen.rs:147), and build.rs generates a third set. Per OD-32, nothing reads the blob's sealed section. The bridge should hydrate its reflection catalog from blob section 3 and delete its own synthesis — otherwise UI codegen has two candidate sources and you're back to drift.

Blocker 3 — OD-32 sealing gaps land first. Sealing currently drops schema fields (signals, guarantees, etc.), there are two blob-dir writers, and no dir manifest/commit point. Generate UI types from the blob before that's fixed and the UI inherits the truncated schema.

One design caveat worth internalizing: the JSON-Schema→proto walk is intentionally lossy — enums, multi-branch unions, and free-form objects degrade to JSON-encoded strings; all integers widen to int64; and no proto3_optional flag is emitted, so Option<scalar> presence is lost (unset vs 0 are indistinguishable on the wire). That's acceptable for transport but wrong as a form-rendering source. So the split should be: SCHEMA_JSON (section 1) drives UI rendering (json_render path — enums, constraints, descriptions survive there), DESCRIPTOR_SET drives wire typing only.

Recommended order: (1) bridge reads blob descriptors + mounts typed services, deleting its duplicate synthesis; (2) an obs.* export command dumps the catalog descriptor set; (3) repoint proto:gen at --descriptor_set_in; (4) hash-pin + runtime drift check; (5) delete the hand-maintained protos — including the six for services that should be plugins anyway. Quick Start

Your CLI should be ready to go at this point.

Context
Before running any commands, a context has to be set which stores the API endpoint information. This allows the CLI to know which server to communicate with, and the user account to use.

NMCLI supports connecting to both standalone (self-hosted) and SaaS(managed) tenants. This is specified with a flag. More details below.

Connecting to standalone (self-hosted) tenants

Assuming your tenant is hosted at https://api.netmaker.example.com

You can use your username and password that you use to sign in to the dashboard UI to set the context. Then you can set the CLI to use that context.

nmctl context set <context name> --endpoint=https://api.netmaker.example.com  --username=<username> --password=<password>  # create the context
nmctl context use <context name>  # apply the created context
plaintext
You can also authenticate via OAuth with the following:

nmctl context set <context name> --endpoint=https://api.netmaker.example.com  --sso  # create the context for OAuth (Social Sign On)
nmctl context use <context name>  # apply the created context
plaintext
Connecting to SaaS (managed) tenants

You can also authenticate with a managed (SaaS) tenant with the following commands:

nmctl context set <context name> --saas --tenant_id=<tenant ID> --username=<username> --password=<password>  # create the context
nmctl context use <context name>  # apply the created context
plaintext

nmctl context set <context name> --saas --sso --tenant_id=<tenant ID>  # create the context for OAuth (Social Sign On)
nmctl context use <context name>  # apply the created context
plaintext
List and switch between contexts

You can see a list of all your contexts that you have created with the following:

nmctl context list
plaintext
That list also tells you what context/tenant is currently selected.

You can switch to a different context by using the use subcommand:

nmctl context use <context name>
plaintext
Delete contexts

You can delete a context with the following:

nmctl context delete <context name>

any of this useful?Using a Btrfs loop file (blob) is an excellent architectural choice for this specific use case.
When your build mechanism generates binaries with [built-in Tonic gRPC server reflection](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic/blob/master/examples/src/reflection/server.rs), the compilation pipelines typically embed a heavy FileDescriptorSet binary blob directly into the compiled artifact. Coupling a Btrfs blob with Incus creates a highly optimized pipeline for managing these specific types of microservice images. [1, 2] 
## Why This Combination Excels for Your Use Case
Using a Btrfs blob perfectly complements a Tonic reflection build pattern in several key ways:
## 1. Instantaneous Copy-on-Write (CoW) Subvolumes
During continuous integration or automated testing, you will likely create dozens of ephemeral container instances from your base microservice image. Because Incus natively leverages Btrfs subvolumes, launching a new container does not copy the large compiled Rust binary or its embedded reflection sets. Instead, it creates an instantaneous, zero-cost pointer clone. [3] 
## 2. Native btrfs send/receive Portability
A key reason to wrap your rootfs pool into a standalone .img blob is that the entire storage environment is encapsulated into a single file. You can easily export test containers, production-ready microservice states, or base rootfs environments using [btrfs send and receive mechanisms](https://github.com/lxc/incus/issues/1549) to replicate the environment across different physical host architectures without breaking your automation pipelines.
## 3. Efficient Storage for Repeated Artifacts
Tonic/Prost compilation pipelines can generate large binaries due to statically linked runtimes and heavy proto serialization structures. Btrfs allows you to enable transparent filesystem compression on the loop pool itself. This forces the embedded reflection data and binary structures to compress cleanly on the fly: [4] 

incus storage set <your-btrfs-pool> btrfs.mount_options "compress=zstd:3"

------------------------------
## Crucial Optimization Step
To prevent the performance degradation mentioned earlier while utilizing a loop file on a host OS, ensure you disable Copy-on-Write for the host-level .img file itself before provisioning it in Incus. This allows the host to treat the blob like raw disk sectors, while the container layers inside the blob still fully utilize Btrfs's native subvolume features: [5] 

# 1. Create your empty target blob file
truncate -s 50G /path/to/host/incus_rootfs.img
# 2. Disable CoW at the host level on that specific file (Crucial!)
chattr +C /path/to/host/incus_rootfs.img
# 3. Format and link to Incus
mkfs.btrfs /path/to/host/incus_rootfs.img
incus storage create tonic-pool btrfs source=/path/to/host/incus_rootfs.img
